review_basis: Original SAP Module 01 numbered WebP slides individually inspected, with diagrams and actual examples followed in display order.
part_title: Cognito, OAuth and Tenant-Aware Application Authorization

scenes.title: Cognito user pools authenticate app users
scenes.visual_overview: A customer signs in to a Cognito user pool, receives identity and access tokens, and an application API separately validates token claims and tenant permissions.
visual_walkthrough: Customer signs in from left
Cognito user pool issues ID and access tokens with different purposes
Application passes relevant access token to API
API validates issuer, audience or client context, expiry and required scopes or claims
Backend checks tenant authorization before allowing request
scenes.visual_example: A valid customer token is not enough to see another customer's data: the API must verify tenant and object ownership.
scenes.visual_synthesis: User pools provide authentication and tokens; business-resource authorization belongs to the application.
scenes.narration: This picture shows how a Cognito user pool signs in a customer without automatically granting every application action. Start at the customer on the left, who authenticates through the user pool. The two token boxes distinguish an ID token containing user identity information from an access token intended for authorization decisions at supported application APIs. Follow the arrows into the application and then the API on the right. The API validates the appropriate token signature and issuer, time validity, intended token context and any required scopes or claims. But the final green box adds a separate business decision: is this user actually allowed to access this tenant's resource? A valid sign-in token does not mean Alice can read Bob's order. The application must enforce ownership or tenant isolation. Nor does the sign-in token itself provide AWS IAM credentials. For the exam, separate the user pool's authentication role from the API's business authorization rules.

scenes.title: Identity pools broker limited AWS credentials
scenes.visual_overview: A user-pool or external identity token flows through a Cognito identity pool to select an authorized role and issue temporary AWS credentials to an app client.
visual_walkthrough: External identity provider or Cognito user pool provides sign-in token
Token delivered to Cognito identity pool
Identity pool chooses configured IAM role and obtains temporary credentials
Mobile app uses credentials to upload to its own S3 prefix
Warning against static permanent keys in mobile client
scenes.visual_example: A mobile app uploads photographs only to its assigned S3 key prefix using an appropriately scoped temporary role session.
scenes.visual_synthesis: A user pool authenticates; an identity pool provides AWS credentials within the configured role and resource restrictions.
scenes.narration: This slide extends the previous customer sign-in case. On the left, the customer authenticates with a user pool or supported external identity provider. The resulting token moves to the Cognito identity pool in the center. The identity pool maps that authenticated identity to an authorized IAM role, using configured role-mapping rules. AWS provides temporary credentials for that role instead of embedding permanent access keys in the mobile application. Follow the return arrow to the phone, then the green arrow to the S3 bucket. The sample application is allowed to upload only into its own permitted object prefix, provided the IAM and S3 policies actually enforce that boundary. This does not make all S3 paths available to every signed-in customer. The red box explicitly rules out long-term AWS access keys in a distributed app. The architecture decision is simple: use user pools for customer authentication and identity pools when that client genuinely needs limited AWS API access.

scenes.title: OAuth 2.0 delegates API access
scenes.visual_overview: Two authorization flows are contrasted: authorization code with PKCE for a public app and client credentials for machine-to-machine access, with ID and access tokens serving different purposes.
visual_walkthrough: Upper row: resource owner, public client, authorization server and resource server
Authorization code and PKCE verifier exchange for token after login
API request carries access token and resource server validates scopes
Lower row: confidential workload uses client credentials without end user
Bottom panels distinguish OIDC ID token, OAuth access token and unrelated IAM role
scenes.visual_example: A mobile app uses authorization code plus PKCE on behalf of a user, while a backend service uses client credentials to access a scoped API without an end-user login.
scenes.visual_synthesis: OAuth grants scoped API access through the appropriate flow; it does not itself assign an AWS IAM role.
scenes.narration: This slide compares two common OAuth 2.0 patterns. Start with the upper row, authorization code with PKCE, intended for a browser or mobile public client acting for a user. The user authenticates through the authorization server, the client receives an authorization code, and exchanges it with a matching PKCE verifier for an access token. The API, or resource server, validates that access token and its scopes. PKCE helps protect the code exchange against interception. Now look at the lower row. A confidential backend client can request an access token using its own client credentials; no end user is involved, so this is machine-to-machine authorization. At the bottom, the token comparison matters: an OIDC ID token conveys authentication information to the client, while an OAuth access token authorizes access to the intended API. The final box warns that OAuth roles such as resource owner and authorization server are not AWS IAM roles. Choose the flow based on whether a user is present and whether the client can securely hold credentials.

scenes.title: Three boundaries, three questions
scenes.visual_overview: A multi-tenant order request crosses user authentication, application authorization and IAM authorization for the backend's AWS resources; the worked example shows allowed and denied tenant paths.
visual_walkthrough: Left pane Alice signs in with Cognito or external identity provider and carries tenant A claims
Middle pane API Gateway/backend verifies access token and enforces order ownership
Right pane backend execution IAM role accesses scoped DynamoDB and S3 resources
Bottom green request for tenants/A/orders/42 succeeds when tenant and ownership checks match
Bottom red request for tenants/B/orders/42 is denied with 403 before any AWS resource call
scenes.visual_example: Alice from tenant A can read an authorized order belonging to tenant A, but a request to tenant B's order is rejected by application policy even if the backend IAM role technically has database read access.
scenes.visual_synthesis: Enforce defense in depth: token validation, tenant/object ownership checks, and least-privilege AWS permissions are separate boundaries.
scenes.narration: This larger diagram connects the complete authentication and authorization story using a multi-tenant order API. Read the three panels from left to right. First, Alice from tenant A signs in using Cognito or an external provider and sends a valid access token. That answers who signed in. Second, the API validates the token and checks whether Alice is authorized for the requested order, including tenant and object ownership. Third, if approved, the backend uses its narrowly scoped IAM execution role to call DynamoDB or S3. IAM determines what AWS resources the backend may access; it cannot by itself establish whether Alice owns order forty-two. Follow the two example rows at the bottom. The green path requests tenant A's authorized order and proceeds after the checks pass. The red path requests tenant B's order and returns HTTP four-oh-three without calling AWS. The bottom warning is the main architecture decision: enforce application-level ownership before resource access, and independently restrict the backend IAM role. Neither a valid login nor an IAM allow replaces tenant isolation.
